manual/code/Runtime/Random/IRandomFuncti.title: IRandomFunction | Unity 6 Core Framework
manual/code/Runtime/Random/IRandomFuncti.summary: IRandomFunction<TIndex, TSeed> Source: ./Runtime/Random/IRandomFunction.cs Overview IRandomFunction<TIndex, TSeed> defines the interface contract for any deterministic random function or RNG used within CoreFramework. It abstracts over index-based and seed-based noise functions (e.g. SquirrelNoise, SecureNoise) so that both stateless and stateful RNGs can be plugged into the same systems. Implementations (like SquirrelNoise64Rng) provide a deterministic, Burst-friendly, and reproducible source of random values for procedural content generation. Key Responsibilities Exposes the Seed and Position (or index) that drive random sequence generation. Provides a consistent API to: Reset or reseed the generator. Query the current Seed value. Step through a sequence deterministically. Retrieve single values or structured values (vectors, rotations). Designed to work with Unity.Mathematics types and Burst. Typical Interface Members Although the interface is generic, your implementing RNGs usually include: Member Purpose Seed { get; } Underlying seed controlling randomness. Position Current index/position (for sequential RNGs). ResetSeed(seed, position) Re-initialize seed & index. Range(min, max) Get a random value in a specified range. Value Normalized float [0,1] per step. InsideUnitSphere / OnUnitSphere Random directions/points. Rotation / RotationUniform Random quaternions. Uint128 / Uint64 etc. Raw integer lanes from noise. Concrete examples can be seen in SquirrelNoise64Rng. Example Usage using CoreFramework.Random; public class Example { public void Demo(IRandomFunction<ulong, ulong> rng) { // reseed rng.ResetSeed(1234UL); // get normalized float float val = rng.Value; // random int range int dice = rng.Range(1, 7); // random rotation var q = rng.RotationUniform; } } Related API [xref:CoreFramework.Random.IRandomFunction](xref:CoreFramework.Random.IRandomFunction<TIndex, TSeed>) xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise64Rng xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise64Bit xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise32Bit xref:CoreFramework.Random.HashBasedNoiseUtils xref:Unity.Mathematics.float3 xref:Unity.Mathematics.quaternion

manual/code/Runtime/Random/NoiseRngUtils.title: NoiseRngUtils | Unity 6 Core Framework
manual/code/Runtime/Random/NoiseRngUtils.summary: NoiseRngUtils Source: ./Runtime/Random/NoiseRngUtils.cs Overview NoiseRngUtils is a helper utility class that bundles common patterns and convenience functions for CoreFramework’s noise-based random number generators. It provides a shared toolkit for implementing IRandomFunction<TIndex,TSeed> RNGs such as SquirrelNoise32Rng and SquirrelNoise64Rng. Use it to reduce boilerplate when writing new RNGs: the static methods encapsulate repeated math for range mapping, normalized float conversions, vector sampling, and direction/rotation utilities. Key Responsibilities Value mapping: Convert raw noise lanes to normalized floats or scaled ranges. Sampling helpers: Produce inside/on unit sphere directions, 2D/3D random points, quaternions. Utility sugar: Step or reseed your RNG consistently across implementations. Performance: All methods are [MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining)] and Burst-friendly. Typical Methods Method Purpose float To01(uint v) Convert uint noise lane to [0,1]. float Range01(uint v, float min, float max) Map noise lane to [min,max]. float2 Direction2D(uint a, uint b) Random 2D unit direction from two lanes. float3 Direction3D(uint a, uint b, uint c) Random 3D unit direction from three lanes. quaternion RotationUniform(uint a, uint b, uint c, uint d) Uniform random quaternion from four lanes. (Exact signatures depend on the utility version you have, but these are the patterns you’ll find.) Example Usage using CoreFramework.Random; public class Example { public void Demo() { // raw lanes from a noise RNG uint a = 123456789u; uint b = 987654321u; // convert to normalized float float val = NoiseRngUtils.To01(a); // get a random direction var dir2 = NoiseRngUtils.Direction2D(a, b); // map to a custom range float roll = NoiseRngUtils.Range01(a, 1f, 6f); } } Related API xref:CoreFramework.Random.NoiseRngUtils [xref:CoreFramework.Random.IRandomFunction](xref:CoreFramework.Random.IRandomFunction<TIndex, TSeed>) xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise32Rng xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise64Rng xref:CoreFramework.Random.HashBasedNoiseUtils xref:Unity.Mathematics.float2 · xref:Unity.Mathematics.float3 · xref:Unity.Mathematics.quaternion

manual/code/Runtime/Random/NoiseType.htm.title: NoiseType | Unity 6 Core Framework
manual/code/Runtime/Random/NoiseType.htm.summary: NoiseType Source: ./Runtime/Random/NoiseType.cs Overview NoiseType is an enumeration that specifies which mixing / hashing algorithm a CoreFramework noise generator or RNG should use. It acts as a runtime switch inside SquirrelNoise32Bit, SquirrelNoise64Bit, and their RNG wrappers, allowing you to pick between multiple bit-mangling strategies (balanced Murmur3 style, rotational, ChaCha quarter rounds, etc.). This gives you fine control over the statistical distribution and performance characteristics of your procedural noise / random functions. Members Enum Value Description MangledBitsShiftXOR A fast, old-school XOR+shift+Murmur mix. MangledBitsBalancedMix Balanced Murmur3-inspired mixing (default). MangledBitsRotational Rotational bit-mangling variant for extra diffusion. ChaChaQuarterRoundSimple Simple ChaCha-inspired quarter-round. ChaChaQuarterRoundAdvanced Full ChaCha-style quarter-round with extra mixing. (Exact names depend on the version of NoiseType.cs you have; these are the standard ones.) Typical Usage using CoreFramework.Random; public class Example { public void Demo() { // pick a mixing style NoiseType type = NoiseType.ChaChaQuarterRoundAdvanced; // feed it into a noise function uint noise = SquirrelNoise32Bit.Get1DNoise(1234, 5678, type); // or into a noise-based RNG var rng = new SquirrelNoise32Rng(0u, 123u, type); float value = rng.Value; // uses selected NoiseType internally } } Related API xref:CoreFramework.Random.NoiseType xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise32Bit xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise64Bit xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise32Rng xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise64Rng xref:CoreFramework.Random.HashBasedNoiseUtils

manual/code/Runtime/Random/NoiseTypes.ht.title: What each noise “type” actually is | Unity 6 Core Framework
manual/code/Runtime/Random/NoiseTypes.ht.summary: What each noise “type” actually is Shared knobs you’ll see a lot Amplitude (amp): vertical scale of the output. output scale. Frequency (freq): how quickly the pattern changes per unit distance. feature size. Octaves: how many stacked layers you sum (each higher octave is smaller scale + lower amplitude). Lacunarity: frequency multiplier per octave (commonly 2.0). Gain / Persistence: amplitude multiplier per octave (commonly 0.5). Think of an octave stack (also called fBm) as your “how bumpy” control; the base noise function you stack (Perlin, value, Simplex, Worley) sets the character of those bumps. Core bases Perlin / Simplex (gradient noise) Produce smooth, band‑limited noise with no sharp grid artifacts. Perlin is lattice‑based; Simplex uses tetrahedra (faster in higher dimensions and easier for analytic derivatives). Output: ~[-1,1]. Great general‑purpose base for terrain, textures. Value noise (hash‑smoothed) Uses a hash to get a value at lattice points, then smooth‑interpolates. With the right fade curve it’s visually similar to Perlin and plays nicely with stateless PRNGs (perfect for your Squirrel functions). Worley / Cellular Computes distance to nearest/2nd‑nearest feature points in each cell; outputs distance patterns → “cells/cracks/pebbles/veins.” Not a heightfield by itself; you usually remap/distort it (invert, take min/max, combine with fBm). Fractal “variants” (they’re just post‑processes / combinations) fBm (Fractional Brownian Motion) Sum octaves of a base noise (Perlin/value/Simplex). Parameters: octaves, lacunarity (≈2), gain (≈0.5). Output looks like classic rolling mountains. Billow billow(p) = abs(base(p)) (then optionally re‑center). Rounds valleys into puffy hills. Stack with fBm parameters → “cloudy” terrain. Ridge / Ridged‑Multi ridge(p) = 1 - abs(base(p)) then sharpen via squaring and biasing. Creates sharp crests; typical for alpine ridges/canyons. Domain warping Feed noise into the coordinates of another noise: base(p + warp(p)*strength). Breaks repetition, creates flow/“river‑like” structures, gnarly cliffs when used with ridges. Analytical derivatives Some gradient noises can return (value, ∂value/∂x, ∂value/∂y, …) cheaply. Use derivatives to modulate detail by slope (e.g., reduce high‑frequency detail on steep slopes → pseudo‑erosion). If your base doesn’t expose derivatives, you can approximate with tiny central differences (still stateless & random‑access). Sean Murray’s “Uber Noise” (No Man’s Sky) A parameterized blender that mixes ridge/billow/base, applies domain warps, and damps by slope/altitude using derivatives. Think: one function with knobs for sharpness, slope erosion, altitude damping, warp strength, plus the usual fBm controls. Squirrel Noise already has the right architectural constraint: stateless, random‑access. Quick mapping: Squirrel → mental recipes Perlin / Simplex: the base (use our smoothed value noise if you don’t have them). fBm: how you stack (octaves, lacunarity, gain). Billow: abs post‑process of the base (then center). Ridge: 1 - abs with sharpening (then stack). Worley: nearest‑point distance field (use f1, f2, or f2-f1 then remap). Analytical derivatives: value + gradient; use to damp high‑freq on steep slopes. Domain warping: warp coordinates with another fBm (one or two stages) before sampling. Sean Murray’s Uber Noise: a single function that blends base/billow/ridge, applies domain warp, and damps by slope/altitude—implemented above as Uber. Perlin (gradient noise) What it is: Smooth scalar field built by dotting pseudo-random gradients at lattice corners with the local offset, then easing and trilinearly blending. Feels like: Rolling hills; smooth, band-limited variations. Knobs: frequency (feature size), output scale (amplitude), seed. Continuity: C1 (value + first derivative continuous). Where it shines: Terrain height, clouds, masks, normals (with analytic grad). Gotchas: Axis-aligned if overused; periodic artifacts if you upsample too far. In Unity6CoreFramework.Random lib: Perlin(…), PerlinWithDerivatives(…) (2D/3D core + analytic grad). Simplex (skewed gradient noise) What it is: Perlin’s sibling on a simplex (triangles/tetrahedra) grid; fewer corners sampled → faster, isotropic patterns. Feels like: Similar to Perlin but slightly “crisper,” less axial bias. Knobs: Same as Perlin. Continuity: C1 (like Perlin). Where it shines: Higher dimensions and cheaper/per-octave use. Gotchas: Patent history (now expired); beware non-standard gradient sets. In Unity6CoreFramework.Random lib: Simplex(x,y,…), Simplex(x,y,z,…) via hash callbacks—no perm tables. fBm (fractal Brownian motion) What it is: Sum of octaves of a base noise at increasing frequency (×lacunarity) and decreasing amplitude (×gain). Feels like: Self-similar detail across scales; “natural” fractal roughness. Knobs: octaves, lacunarity (≈2), gain (≈0.5), base frequency/amplitude. Where it shines: Mountains, rough textures, masks. Gotchas: Dynamic range grows with octaves → normalize if you want stable [-1,1]. In Unity6CoreFramework.Random lib: FBm(baseFn, …); wrappers: SquirrelNoise32Bit.FBm, …64Bit.FBm. Billow (abs fBm) What it is: fBm of abs(base), remapped back to [-1,1] per octave. Feels like: Puffy, soft pillows; clouds, rolling dunes. Knobs: Same as fBm (abs makes peaks symmetric). Where it shines: Soft cloud cover, fog density, soft ground. Gotchas: Can look too “round” without mixing with other components. In Unity6CoreFramework.Random lib: Billow(baseFn, …) + 32/64 wrappers. Ridge (ridged multifractal) What it is: Invert and sharpen the absolute value per octave; weight by previous octave. Feels like: Sharp crests, deep valleys—mountain ranges, cracked rock. Knobs: ridgeOffset (~1), ridgeSharpness (≥2), plus fBm knobs. Where it shines: Mountain masks, glacial spines, canyons. Gotchas: Over-sharpening can cause ringing; modulate gain/weight for stability. In Unity6CoreFramework.Random lib: Ridge(baseFn, …) + wrappers. Worley / Cellular What it is: For each sample, find nearest “feature point” in nearby lattice cells; return distances: F1 (nearest), F2 (2nd), combos like F2−F1. Feels like: Cells, plates, cracks, pebble patterns depending on metric/jitter. Knobs: metric (Euclidean/Manhattan/Chebyshev), jitter (0=centered, 1=free), frequency. Where it shines: Stone, scales, cell membranes, road networks (with post-ops). Gotchas: Value range depends on metric/scale; usually normalize or use F2−F1. In Unity6CoreFramework.Random lib: Cellular2DCore/3DCore + Cellular2D/3D, CellularF1, F2MinusF1. Worley / Cellular = “worms” vs “blocky” Wormy (veins, tunnels, tendrils) Idea: Use Euclidean distance with higher jitter, then emphasize cell edges via F2 - F1, optionally warp the domain so edges bend and weave. Metric: Euclidean Jitter: 0.75–1.0 (features roam inside the cell → organic) Frequency: start low (big features), e.g. 0.002–0.01 in world units Value to use: edge = F2 - F1 (small near edges) → turn into a bright line with an inverse/smoothstep Warping: Apply a low-frequency Domain Warp first to curve the edges Nice remaps: vein = 1 - saturate((F2-F1)/w) (thin veins; w ~ 0.05–0.2 in cell units) vein = exp(-k*(F2-F1)) for smoother, exponential falloff (k ~ 5–15) Tips Increase jitter for more organic meanders; reduce edgeWidth for thinner/wilder veins. Warp twice (two different seeds/freqs) for “arteries + capillaries”. For cave/tunnel generation: threshold vein > t and run connectivity post-process. Blocky (cells, tiles, city/brick vibes) Idea: Choose Manhattan or Chebyshev metrics and keep jitter low so features anchor near cell centers. Edges become straight, grid-like. Metric: Manhattan → diamond/orthogonal facets Chebyshev → square/box facets Jitter: 0.0–0.25 (structured, centered) Frequency: 0.003–0.02 (depending on desired tile size) Value to use: F1 (distance to nearest site) for rounded cells, or F2 - F1 for sharp edges Post: quantize or step to get hard tiling; mix with fBm to add texture variation in each cell. Tips Manhattan + low jitter is great for streets/blocks; extrude edges as walls. Use the cell id (r.Cell) to seed a per-cell color/height: cellSeed = SquirrelNoise32Bit.Get2DNoise(r.Cell.x, r.Cell.y, seed) then modulate fBm. Analytical Derivatives (∇noise) What it is: Closed-form gradient of Perlin/Simplex w.r.t. position (not finite diff). Feels like: A vector field pointing “uphill” in the scalar noise. Knobs: None—just pick the base noise & scale via frequency. Where it shines: Flow maps, erosion simulation, normals, advection, curl fields. Gotchas: Make sure your grad matches your exact fade/grad definitions. In Unity6CoreFramework.Random lib: PerlinWithDeriv(…) (2D/3D) returning (value, grad). Domain Warping (a.k.a. position warp) What it is: Displace the input position by a low-frequency vector field before sampling another (or same) noise. x' = x + A * Wx(x), y' = y + A * Wy(x), z' = z + A * Wz(x) Feels like: Twisted, folded patterns; veins, flowy marbling, rivers. Knobs: Warp amplitude, warp frequency/octaves (warp*), then value stack knobs. Where it shines: Breaking grid-like appearance, creating coherent features. Gotchas: Large amplitude at high frequency can “tear” features; start small, low-freq. In Unity6CoreFramework.Random lib: DomainWarp(baseFn, …) (warps with three independent stacks). “Uber Noise” (NMS-style composition) What it is: A recipe: stacked warps → fBm base → subtract a ridged component → clamp/normalize. Feels like: Big shapes with believable micro detail; planetary-scale variation that holds up close. Knobs: Two warp blocks (warp1/warp2 Amp/Freq/Octaves), fBm (octaves/freq/gain/lacunarity), ridge mix. Where it shines: Biomes, planet surfaces, large-to-small continuity. Gotchas: Many knobs—tune in stages: warp1 (big), warp2 (medium), fBm, then ridge. In Unity6CoreFramework.Random lib: UberNoise(baseFn, …) (both seeds). Cross-cutting parameters (quick map) frequency: feature size (↑frequency → smaller features). Often start at 1 and scale your input position instead. amplitude: output scale per octave (top-level). octaves: number of layers in the stack. lacunarity: frequency multiplier per octave (≈2). gain: amplitude multiplier per octave (≈0.5). jitter (Worley): 0 = features centered, 1 = fully random inside cell. Stateless integration pattern (how Unity6CoreFramework.Random code lines up) Base scalar field: Perlin(...) or Simplex(...) returning ~[-1,1]. Fractals: FBm/Billow/Ridge(baseFn, p, seed, …). Gradients: use PerlinWithDerivatives (no extra samples). Cellular: Cellular2D/3D → use F1, F2, F2−F1 or feature positions. Warps: DomainWarp(baseFn, …) then feed into another stack (as in UberNoise). The two axes to keep straight Base field (what pattern you’re sampling) Perlin / Simplex (gradient noise) Cellular / Worley (distance-to-features) (Optional) Value noise (hash values + smooth fade-lerp) Entropy core (how hash integers to “random”) NoiseType enum: MangledBits*, ChaCha* This only changes the bit-mixing used to produce corner hashes / feature jitter. It doesn’t change the macro algorithm—Perlin is still Perlin, Worley is still Worley. Shared knobs (quick) frequency = feature size; amplitude = output scale; octaves/lacunarity/gain = fractal stack controls; jitter/metric = Worley flavoring. How each concept maps to Squirrel Noise code Concept Core (low-level) 32-bit wrappers 64-bit wrappers Range Notes Perlin 2D HashBasedNoiseUtils.Perlin(xf,yf,h00,h10,h01,h11) SquirrelNoise32Bit.Perlin(x,y, seed, type) SquirrelNoise64Bit.Perlin(x,y, seed, type) ~[-1,1] Corner hashes come from Get2DNoise. Perlin 3D HashBasedNoiseUtils.Perlin(xf,yf,zf, …8 hashes…) SquirrelNoise32Bit.Perlin(x,y,z, seed, type) SquirrelNoise64Bit.Perlin(x,y,z, seed, type) ~[-1,1] Same idea, 8 corners. Perlin + analytic ∇ (2D) HashBasedNoiseUtils.PerlinWithDeriv(xf,yf,…, out float2 d) SquirrelNoise32Bit.PerlinWithDeriv(x,y, seed, out float2 d, type) SquirrelNoise64Bit.PerlinWithDeriv(x,y, seed, out float2 d, type) value ~[-1,1] Exact gradient, no extra samples. Perlin + analytic ∇ (3D) HashBasedNoiseUtils.PerlinWithDeriv(xf,yf,zf,…, out float3 d) SquirrelNoise32Bit.PerlinWithDeriv(x,y,z, seed, out float3 d, type) SquirrelNoise64Bit.PerlinWithDeriv(x,y,z, seed, out float3 d, type) value ~[-1,1] Value & Grad aliases – SquirrelNoise32Bit.ValueAndGrad(...) SquirrelNoise64Bit.ValueAndGrad(...) – Just forwards to PerlinWithDeriv. Finite-diff gradient – SquirrelNoise32Bit.GradientCentral(float2/float3, seed, eps, type) SquirrelNoise64Bit.GradientCentral(float2/float3, seed, eps, type) – Uses central differences (extra samples). Simplex 2D (inside Simplex code: skew/unskew + Grad2Vec) SquirrelNoise32Bit.Simplex2DCore(pos, seed, freq, type) SquirrelNoise64Bit.Simplex2DCore(pos, seed, freq, type) ~[-1,1] No perm tables; hashes via Squirrel. Simplex 3D (skew/unskew + Grad3Vec) SquirrelNoise32Bit.Simplex3DCore(pos, seed, freq, type) SquirrelNoise64Bit.Simplex3DCore(pos, seed, freq, type) ~[-1,1] Cellular/Worley 2D – SquirrelNoise32Bit.Cellular2D(...) SquirrelNoise64Bit.Cellular2D(...) F1/F2 in cell units Use metric + jitter; feature pos/cell returned too. Cellular/Worley 3D – SquirrelNoise32Bit.Cellular3D(...) SquirrelNoise64Bit.Cellular3D(...) F1/F2 in cell units Cellular helpers NormalizeF101 / NormalizeF1Inv01 / CellularVein01 / CellularVeinExp01 CellularF1 / CellularF2MinusF1 / CellularEdge01 / CellularEdgeExp01 / CellularEdgeSigned same 0..1 or [-1,1] Quickly get fills/edges/veins. fBm – SquirrelNoise32Bit.FBm(p, seed, oct, freq, amp, lac, gain, normalize, type) SquirrelNoise64Bit.FBm(p, seed, oct, freq, amp, lac, gain, normalize, type) ~[-1,1] (when normalized) Stacks Perlin underneath (via your wrapper). Billow – SquirrelNoise32Bit.Billow(...) SquirrelNoise64Bit.Billow(...) ~[-1,1] Uses abs(base) per octave. Ridge – SquirrelNoise32Bit.Ridge(...) SquirrelNoise64Bit.Ridge(...) ~[-1,1] Invert+sharpen, octave-weighted. Domain warp – SquirrelNoise32Bit.DomainWarp(...) SquirrelNoise64Bit.DomainWarp(...) scalar Builds a low-freq vector warp then samples fBm. Uber Noise – SquirrelNoise32Bit.UberNoise(...) SquirrelNoise64Bit.UberNoise(...) [-1,1] Two warps → fBm → subtract ridges → clamp. The Diffrence between 32Bit and 64Bit is 32Bit uses uint for the seed and int for the positions, where 64Bit uses ulong for the seed and positions. The Squirrel “NoiseType” mixers (entropy core) These feed all the “get hash” calls (Get1D/2D/3DNoise in 32-bit, GetUInt64/… in 64-bit), which in turn feed: Perlin/Simplex (corner hashes → gradient selection) Cellular (cell seeds → jitter vectors) Any per-octave reseeding (MixOctave helpers) Pick: MangledBitsBalancedMix (default): great avalanche, stable. MangledBitsShiftXOR / MangledBitsRotational: slightly different bias/dispersion; good for decorrelating layers. ChaChaQuarterRoundSimple/Advanced: strong diffusion; nice if you want “very random” local variation. Mental model: Changing NoiseType is like swapping the hash function under the hood—it alters micro-texture and correlation, not the high-level pattern that Perlin/Simplex/Cellular produce. Defaults that “just work” fBm: octaves=5–7, lacunarity=2.0, gain=0.5, normalize output. Ridge: ridgeOffset≈1.0, ridgeSharpness=2–3, freq ×1.2–1.6 vs base. Cellular “wormy”: Euclidean, jitter=0.8–1.0, edgeWidth≈0.1 (2D), 0.12 (3D). Cellular “blocky”: Chebyshev or Manhattan, jitter=0.0–0.2. fBm Start: octaves=5–7, lacunarity=2, gain=0.5, frequency≈0.001–0.01 Bigger features: ↓frequency or ↓octaves Finer detail: ↑octaves (normalize output to keep range stable —Squirrel Noise stacks already do) Rougher surface: ↑lacunarity (2→2.2) or ↓gain (0.5→0.45) Smoother surface: ↓lacunarity (1.9) or ↑gain (0.55) Billow (puffy) Start: same as fBm; often gain=0.55–0.65 More “pillow”: ↑gain (amplitudes decay slower) Less symmetric/too soft? Mix in a little standard fBm (0.7*Billow + 0.3*fBm) Ridge (mountainous) Start: ridgeOffset≈1.0, ridgeSharpness≈2.0–3.0, frequency slightly higher than fBm (×1.2–1.6) Sharper spines: ↑ridgeSharpness (2→3.5) Chunkier ridges: ↑ridgeOffset above 1 (1.1–1.3) Too spiky? ↓ridgeSharpness or ↓frequency Mixing Cellular with the fractals Wormy rivers over terrain Get terrain base: height = FBm(Perlin, p3, seed, …) Get vein mask from Cellular (Euclidean, jitter high): vein ∈ [0,1] Carve: height -= vein * carveDepth Optional: domain warp the vein sampling position with a very low-frequency warp so rivers meander. Blocky biomes Use Cellular2D with Chebyshev, jitter≈0.05 Compute a cell id → pick biome params (different seeds/gains/octaves) Evaluate fBm/Billow/Ridge per biome to keep features consistent within cells and distinct between cells. Cell edges as roads Threshold F2-F1 < w, then run a thinning/skeletonization if needed. With Manhattan, you get orthogonal “city blocks” almost for free. Domain warping with helpers Big bend, small twist: warp amps small (0.2–0.8), warp frequencies lower than the value frequency. Two-scale warp (“Uber Noise”): a slow, strong warp (shape), then a faster, weaker warp (detail), then the fBm stack. Squirrel Noise has already codified this in UberNoise. Final tuning heuristics (quick cheatsheet) Want straighter structure? ↓jitter, switch to Manhattan/Chebyshev. Want more organic curves? ↑jitter, keep Euclidean, add 1–2 domain warps. Thinner lines (worms/roads)? ↓edgeWidth (or ↑k in the exponential remap). Bigger cells/roads? ↓frequency. (Remember all distances scale with your sampling frequency.) Too noisy? Lower the value octaves, not the warp octaves. Keep warps smooth. Terrain too mushy? Add a small Ridge layer (2–3 octaves) and mix it in (0.2–0.4). Quick “which one should I use?” guide General terrain/masks: Perlin fBm. Add Ridge (mix 0.2–0.4) for bite. Puffy clouds/sand: Billow (abs fBm). Sharp crests/canyons: Ridge. Veins/river networks: Cellular with F2−F1 → CellularEdge01 (Euclidean, high jitter), optionally domain-warped. Tiles/blocks/streets: Cellular (Chebyshev or Manhattan), low jitter, use F1 or F2−F1 + threshold. Slope-aware detail: Use PerlinWithDeriv and reduce high-freq where |∇| is large.

manual/code/Runtime/Random/NoiseTypesSqu.title: Noise Types & Squirrel Integration — A Practical Guide | Unity 6 Core Framework
manual/code/Runtime/Random/NoiseTypesSqu.summary: Noise Types & Squirrel Integration — A Practical Guide A compact, production-oriented reference that explains what each noise is, how its knobs shape results, and exactly how it maps to SquirrelNoise32Bit / SquirrelNoise64Bit APIs and HashBasedNoiseUtils cores. Shared knobs (you’ll see them everywhere) Amplitude (amp): vertical scale of the output. Frequency (freq): feature size (↑freq → smaller features). Often scale the input position instead. Octaves: how many stacked layers you sum; each octave is higher freq and lower amp. Lacunarity: frequency multiplier per octave (≈ 2.0). Gain / Persistence: amplitude multiplier per octave (≈ 0.5). Think of an octave stack (fBm) as your “how bumpy” control; the base noise you stack (Perlin, Simplex, Value, Worley) sets the character of those bumps. Core bases Perlin / Simplex (gradient noise) What: Pseudo-random gradients at lattice corners, faded and blended. Simplex uses skewed simplices (triangles/tetrahedra), fewer samples in >2D. Feels like: Smooth, band-limited hills; Simplex is slightly crisper and more isotropic. Range: ~[-1, 1]. Continuity: C1 (value + first derivative continuous). Where to use: Terrain height, masks, clouds, normals (with analytic gradients). In Squirrel Noise: 2D/3D value: SquirrelNoise32Bit.Perlin(...), SquirrelNoise64Bit.Perlin(...) Analytic gradient: PerlinWithDeriv(...) (2D/3D) on both 32/64 Simplex cores: Simplex2DCore(...), Simplex3DCore(...) (hash-callback based) Value noise (hash-smoothed) What: Hash lattice values and smooth-interpolate with Fade. Feels like: Perlin-ish; trivial to drive from stateless Squirrel hashes. Note: Already using hash-driven gradients/values under Perlin/Simplex; value noise fits the same pattern if you ever want it. In Squirrel Noise: 1D/2D/3D/4D value: .Get1DNoise(...), .Get2DNoise(...) .Get3DNoise(...) .Get3DNoise(...) .Get4DNoise(...) both 32/64 Worley / Cellular What: Distance to nearest / 2nd-nearest feature points per cell → cells, cracks, pebbles, veins. Not a heightfield by itself: You usually remap (invert, edge extract) or combine with other fields. In Squirrel Noise: .Cellular2D(...), .Cellular3D(...), helpers (CellularF1, CellularF2MinusF1, CellularEdge01, CellularEdgeExp01, CellularEdgeSigned) both 32/64. Fractal “variants” (post-process + stacking) fBm (Fractional Brownian Motion) What: Sum octaves of a base noise at increasing frequency and decreasing amplitude. Feels like: Classic rolling mountains; self-similar detail. Knobs: octaves, lacunarity≈2, gain≈0.5, base freq/amp. In Squirrel Noise: .FBm(...) both 32/64. Billow What: abs(base(p)) per octave, then re-center. Feels like: Puffy pillows / clouds. In Squirrel Noise: .Billow(...) both 32/64. Ridge (Ridged-multifractal) What: r = 1 - abs(base(p)), sharpen via power/bias, weight by previous octave. Feels like: Sharp crests, deep valleys. In Squirrel Noise: .Ridge(...) both 32/64. Domain warping What: Displace input coords by a low-frequency vector field before sampling: p' = p + A * W(p) Feels like: Twisted, meandering structures; breaks grid repetition. In Squirrel Noise: .DomainWarp(...) both 32/64. Analytical derivatives (∇noise) What: Closed-form gradient of Perlin with your exact Fade/grad definitions. Use: Slope-aware detail, normals, flow/advection, curl fields. In Squirrel Noise: PerlinWithDeriv(...) (2D/3D) on both 32/64. Aliases: ValueAndGrad(...). Approximation: GradientCentral(...) (finite differences). “Uber Noise” (No Man’s Sky-style composition) What: Two domain warps → fBm base → subtract a ridged component → clamp/normalize. Feels like: Big shapes with believable micro detail that holds up close. In Squirrel Noise: .UberNoise(...) on both 32/64. Stateless integration pattern (how it all plugs together) Entropy core: NoiseType picks the hash/mixer (see below). Corner/feature hashes: 32-bit: Get1D/2D/3DNoise; 64-bit: GetUInt64, Get2DNoise(...) etc. Per-octave reseed: MixOctave(seed, i) (32/64 variants). Gradient/value cores: HashBasedNoiseUtils.Perlin(...), ...PerlinWithDeriv(...), Simplex2DCore/3DCore. Cellular: Cellular2D/3D returns F1/F2 + feature/cell info; remap with helpers. NoiseType (the hash mixer) enum controls how indices/seeds scramble into pseudo-random bits: Use by default: MangledBitsBalancedMix Alternatives: MangledBitsShiftXOR, MangledBitsRotational (slightly different dispersion), ChaChaQuarterRoundSimple/Advanced (strong diffusion) Mental model: Swapping NoiseType changes micro-texture/correlation, not the high-level algorithm (Perlin/Simplex/Cellular). API map (what to call for what) Concept 32-bit wrapper 64-bit wrapper Low-level core Notes Perlin 2D/3D SquirrelNoise32Bit.Perlin(...) SquirrelNoise64Bit.Perlin(...) HashBasedNoiseUtils.Perlin(...) ~[-1,1] Perlin + ∇ (2D/3D) PerlinWithDeriv(...) PerlinWithDeriv(...) HashBasedNoiseUtils.PerlinWithDeriv(...) Value + gradient Simplex 2D/3D Simplex2DCore/3DCore(...) Simplex2DCore/3DCore(...) (inside cores) ~[-1,1] Cellular 2D/3D Cellular2D/3D(...) Cellular2D/3D(...) – F1/F2 + cell/feature Cellular helpers CellularF1, CellularF2MinusF1, CellularEdge01, CellularEdgeExp01, CellularEdgeSigned same NormalizeF101, CellularVein01, CellularVeinExp01 0..1 or [-1,1] fBm FBm(...) FBm(...) – Normalized to ~[-1,1] Billow Billow(...) Billow(...) – ~[-1,1] Ridge Ridge(...) Ridge(...) – ~[-1,1] Domain Warp DomainWarp(...) DomainWarp(...) – Warp → fBm Uber Noise UberNoise(...) UberNoise(...) – Two warps + fBm − ridge Grad approx GradientCentral(...) GradientCentral(...) – Central differences Cellular = two practical buckets Wormy (veins, tunnels, tendrils) Metric: Euclidean Jitter: 0.75–1.0 (organic) Frequency: low (e.g. 0.002–0.01) Value: use edges → F2 - F1 then invert/soften Warp: optional low-freq warp to bend paths Minimal recipe (2D → [-1,1]): float WorleyWormy2D(float2 P, ulong seed, float freq=0.005f, float jitter=1.0f, float edgeWidth=0.1f) { var r = SquirrelNoise64Bit.Cellular2D(P, seed, frequency: freq, jitter: jitter, metric: HashBasedNoiseUtils.CellularDistance.Euclidean); float vein01 = 1f - math.saturate((r.F2 - r.F1) / edgeWidth); return vein01 * 2f - 1f; } Blocky (tiles, bricks, city grids) Metric: Manhattan (diamond) or Chebyshev (square) Jitter: 0.0–0.25 (anchored) Frequency: 0.003–0.02 Value: F1 for fill, F2−F1 for edges; step/quantize for hard panels Minimal recipe (2D): float WorleyBlocky2D(float2 P, ulong seed, float freq=0.01f, float jitter=0.1f) { var r = SquirrelNoise64Bit.Cellular2D(P, seed, frequency: freq, jitter: jitter, metric: HashBasedNoiseUtils.CellularDistance.Chebyshev); float edges01 = 1f - math.saturate((r.F2 - r.F1) / 0.1f); return edges01 * 2f - 1f; } Fractal defaults (good starting points) fBm octaves=5–7, lacunarity=2, gain=0.5, normalize output. Bigger features: ↓freq or ↓octaves. Finer detail: ↑octaves (keep normalization). Billow Same as fBm; often gain=0.55–0.65. Too round? Mix a bit of plain fBm: 0.7*Billow + 0.3*fBm. Ridge Start: ridgeOffset≈1.0, ridgeSharpness=2–3, frequency ×1.2–1.6 vs base. Too spiky? ↓sharpness or ↓freq. Mixing Cellular with fractals Wormy rivers over terrain height = FBm(Perlin, p, seed, …) vein01 = CellularEdge01(...) (Euclidean, high jitter) height -= vein01 * carveDepth Optional: warp the vein sampling position with a very low-freq warp. Blocky biomes Cellular2D with Chebyshev, jitter≈0.05 Per-cell ID: Get2DNoise(r.Cell.x, r.Cell.y, seed) → pick biome params Evaluate fBm/Billow/Ridge with that per-cell seed. Road masks Threshold F2−F1 < w, optionally thin/skeletonize. Domain warping heuristics Big bend, small twist: keep warp amplitude modest (0.2–0.8), warp freq lower than the value freq. Two-scale warp: slow/strong warp for macro shape, then faster/weaker warp for mid detail. Too torn: reduce warp freq or amplitude. Handy snippets 1) Generic vein mask (01) from a Cellular result [MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining)] static float WorleyVein01(in HashBasedNoiseUtils.Cellular2DResult r, float edgeWidth = 0.1f) => 1f - math.saturate((r.F2 - r.F1) / edgeWidth); 2) 3D wormy with small fractal detail float Worm3D(float3 P, ulong seed) { var r = SquirrelNoise64Bit.Cellular3D(P, seed, frequency: 0.006f, jitter: 0.9f); float vein01 = 1f - math.saturate((r.F2 - r.F1) / 0.12f); float detail = 0.25f * SquirrelNoise64Bit.FBm(P * 1.8f, seed, octaves: 4, gain: 0.55f); return math.saturate(vein01 + detail); } 3) Blocky tiles with per-cell variation float BlockyTile(float2 P, ulong seed) { var r = SquirrelNoise64Bit.Cellular2D(P, seed, frequency: 0.01f, jitter: 0.05f, metric: HashBasedNoiseUtils.CellularDistance.Chebyshev); // Per-cell seed for interior variation: ulong cellSeed = SquirrelNoise64Bit.GetCellSeed2D(r.Cell, seed); float tile = SquirrelNoise64Bit.FBm(new float3(P, 0), cellSeed, octaves: 4, gain: 0.6f); float edges = 1f - math.saturate((r.F2 - r.F1) / 0.08f); return math.clamp(tile * 0.7f + edges * 0.3f, -1f, 1f); } Final tuning cheatsheet Straighter structure: ↓jitter, use Manhattan/Chebyshev. More organic curves: ↑jitter, keep Euclidean, add 1–2 domain warps. Thinner veins/roads: ↓edgeWidth (or ↑k in exponential remap). Bigger cells/roads: ↓frequency (remember F1/F2 are in cell units at your sampling freq). Too noisy: lower the value octaves first; keep warps smooth/low-freq. Terrain mushy: add a small Ridge layer (2–3 octaves, mix 0.2–0.4). Ranges, seeds, performance notes Ranges: Perlin/Simplex are ~[-1,1] (cores match this); Cellular helpers return 0..1 or [-1,1] as named. Seeds: Use MixOctave(seed, i) for decorrelated octave seeds; 32/64 versions exist. NoiseType: Keep MangledBitsBalancedMix unless you need a different micro-texture profile. Unity Burst: All hot paths are AggressiveInlining; keep branches minimal (already do). Prefer float math; avoid allocations. TL;DR Choose base: Perlin/Simplex for smooth, Worley for cells. Shape with fBm/Billow/Ridge. Warp for richness. Use PerlinWithDeriv for slope-aware tricks. Drive everything from stateless Squirrel hashes; swap NoiseType if you want different bit-mix flavor.

manual/code/Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise.title: SquirrelNoise128 | Unity 6 Core Framework
manual/code/Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise.summary: SquirrelNoise128 Source: ./Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise128.cs Overview SquirrelNoise128 provides 128-bit lane hashing utilities used to build deterministic pseudo-random 1D/2D/3D/4D noise. It works with ulong2 (two 64-bit lanes) and returns either packed 128-bit results or reduced 64/32-bit scalars. Float helpers convert to [0,1] or [-1,1] ranges. Default algorithm: NoiseType.ChaChaQuarterRoundSimple (see NoiseType enum). Internally, hashing mixes constants like the 64-bit golden-ratio prime. Core functions 128- / 64-bit ulong2 GetUInt128(ulong2 index, ulong2 seed, NoiseType type = Default) ulong GetUInt64 (ulong2 index, ulong2 seed, NoiseType type = Default) // OR of both lanes Integer noise (returns uint) uint Get1DNoise(ulong2 index, ulong2 seed, NoiseType type = Default) uint Get2DNoise(ulong2 x, ulong2 y, ulong2 seed, NoiseType type = Default) uint Get3DNoise(ulong2 x, ulong2 y, ulong2 z, ulong2 seed, NoiseType type = Default) uint Get4DNoise(ulong2 x, ulong2 y, ulong2 z, ulong2 w, ulong2 seed, NoiseType type = Default) (2D/3D/4D combine coordinates with 64-bit primes before hashing.) Float helpers float Get1DNoise01 (ulong2 index, ulong2 seed, NoiseType type = Default) // [0,1] float Get2DNoise01 (ulong2 x, ulong2 y, ulong2 seed, NoiseType type = Default) float Get3DNoise01 (ulong2 x, ulong2 y, ulong2 z, ulong2 seed, NoiseType type = Default) float Get4DNoise01 (ulong2 x, ulong2 y, ulong2 z, ulong2 w, ulong2 seed, NoiseType type = Default) float Get1DNoiseNeg1To1(ulong2 index, ulong2 seed, NoiseType type = Default) // [-1,1] float Get2DNoiseNeg1To1(ulong2 x, ulong2 y, ulong2 seed, NoiseType type = Default) float Get3DNoiseNeg1To1(ulong2 x, ulong2 y, ulong2 z, ulong2 seed, NoiseType type = Default) float Get4DNoiseNeg1To1(ulong2 x, ulong2 y, ulong2 z, ulong2 w, ulong2 seed, NoiseType = Default) Usage examples 2D tileable sampling (integers-in, floats-out) using CoreFramework.Mathematics; using CoreFramework.Random; int w = 256, h = 256; var seed = new ulong2(12345UL, 67890UL); for (int y = 0; y < h; y++) for (int x = 0; x < w; x++) { // pack coordinates into ulong2 lanes if desired; here we just broadcast var X = new ulong2((ulong)x); var Y = new ulong2((ulong)y); float v01 = SquirrelNoise128.Get2DNoise01(X, Y, seed); // [0,1] // ...write to texture / heightmap... } 3D volume strip (compatible with the editor heatmaps) var seed = (ulong2)(42UL); for (int y = 0; y < H; y++) for (int x = 0; x < W; x++) for (int z = 0; z < W; z++) { float v = SquirrelNoise128.Get3DNoise01((ulong2)(ulong)x, (ulong2)(ulong)y, (ulong2)(ulong)z, seed); // pack at column = z*W + x, row = y } Notes Functions are MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining for Burst friendliness. GetUInt64 reduces GetUInt128 by OR’ing lanes; pick the variant appropriate for your distribution needs. Float mapping helpers use HashBasedNoiseUtils.ToZeroToOne / ToNegOneToOne. Related API xref:CoreFramework.Mathematics.ulong2 xref:CoreFramework.Random.HashBasedNoiseUtils xref:CoreFramework.Random.NoiseType xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise32Bit xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise64Bit

manual/code/Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise.title: SquirrelNoise32Bit | Unity 6 Core Framework
manual/code/Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise.summary: SquirrelNoise32Bit Source: ./Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise32Bit.cs Overview SquirrelNoise32Bit is the 32-bit, hash-based noise core for CoreFramework. It exposes fast, seedable 1D–4D integer noise, normalized float variants ([0,1] and [-1,1]), lightweight Perlin wrappers (2D/3D, with optional analytic derivatives), and Cellular/Worley helpers. Defaults use DefaultNoiseType (currently MangledBitsBalancedMix) — see the guides below for details and trade-offs. Further reading: Noise Types & Squirrel Integration — A Practical Guide What each noise “type” actually is 32-bit integer noise public static uint Get1DNoise(int index, uint seed, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static uint Get2DNoise(int x, int y, uint seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static uint Get3DNoise(int x, int y, int z, uint seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static uint Get4DNoise(int x, int y, int z, int w, uint seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Returns component-hashed uint values; stable across platforms for the same inputs. Normalized (0–1) Variants public static float Get1DNoise01(int index, uint seed, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Get2DNoise01(int x, int y, uint seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Get3DNoise01(int x, int y, int z, uint seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Get4DNoise01(int x, int y, int z, int w, uint seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Same as the integer cores but mapped to [0,1] float. Normalized (−1…1) Variants public static float Get1DNoiseNeg1To1(int index, uint seed, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Get2DNoiseNeg1To1(int x, int y, uint seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Get3DNoiseNeg1To1(int x, int y, int z, uint seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Get4DNoiseNeg1To1(int x, int y, int z, int w, uint seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Same cores, remapped to [-1,1] float. 64-bit and 128-bit helpers public static ulong GetUInt64 (int index, uint seed, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static ulong2 GetUInt128(int index, uint seed, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Build larger hashes from the 32-bit core for wide keys and RNG state. Perlin noise (float domain) Scalar Perlin with corner-hashing done via the selected NoiseType. public static float Perlin(float x, float y, uint seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Perlin(float x, float y, float z, uint seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Perlin + analytic derivatives public static float PerlinWithDeriv(float x, float y, uint seed, out float2 deriv, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float PerlinWithDeriv(float x, float y, float z, uint seed, out float3 deriv, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) // Cell/offset overloads: public static float PerlinWithDeriv(float2 offset, int2 cell, uint seed, out float2 deriv, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float PerlinWithDeriv(float3 offset, int3 cell, uint seed, out float3 deriv, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Derivatives are computed analytically (not finite-differenced). Value noise with gradient public static float ValueAndGrad(float x, float y, uint seed, out float2 grad, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float ValueAndGrad(float2 p, uint seed, out float2 grad, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float ValueAndGrad(float3 p, uint seed, out float3 grad, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Cellular / Worley public static HashBasedNoiseUtils.Cellular2DResult Cellular2D( float x, float y, int frequency, uint seed, float jitter = 0.9f, HashBasedNoiseUtils.CellularDistance metric = HashBasedNoiseUtils.CellularDistance.Euclidean, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static HashBasedNoiseUtils.Cellular3DResult Cellular3D( float x, float y, float z, int frequency, uint seed, float jitter = 0.9f, HashBasedNoiseUtils.CellularDistance metric = HashBasedNoiseUtils.CellularDistance.Euclidean, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Returns nearest/second-nearest distances (F1, F2), feature position, and owning cell. See Cellular remaps and normalization helpers in HashBasedNoiseUtils. Examples using CoreFramework.Random; // integer uint h = SquirrelNoise32Bit.Get3DNoise(12, 7, -4, seed: 1337); // normalized float float n = SquirrelNoise32Bit.Get2DNoise01(128, 64, seed: 42); // Perlin + derivative float v = SquirrelNoise32Bit.PerlinWithDeriv(3.2f, -1.1f, seed: 9, out float2 d); // wide keys ulong k64 = SquirrelNoise32Bit.GetUInt64(5, 99); ulong2 k128 = SquirrelNoise32Bit.GetUInt128(5, 99); Notes All methods are [MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining] and [BurstCompile] ready. Works statelessly — you can query any index without sequential calls. Use NoiseType to switch between bit-mix strategies (MangledBits, ChaCha, etc.). Related API xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise32Bit xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise32Rng xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise64Bit xref:CoreFramework.Random.SquirrelNoise64Rng xref:CoreFramework.Random.HashBasedNoiseUtils xref:CoreFramework.Random.NoiseType xref:CoreFramework.Mathematics.ulong2 xref:Unity.Mathematics.uint Noise Types & Squirrel Integration — A Practical Guide What each noise “type” actually is

manual/code/Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise.title: SquirrelNoise32Rng | Unity 6 Core Framework
manual/code/Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise.summary: SquirrelNoise32Rng Source: ./Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise32Rng.cs Overview SquirrelNoise32Rng is a lightweight, stateless-style RNG façade built on the 32-bit Squirrel noise core. Given a Seed and Position, it produces reproducible random values (scalars, vectors, rotations) by advancing the Position and hashing it with the chosen NoiseType. It’s ideal for deterministic gameplay, spawning, and procedural generation where you want repeatable streams without maintaining a heavy PRNG state. Defaults use NoiseType.MangledBitsBalancedMix. See the guides for trade-offs and picking a noise type. Further reading: Noise Types & Squirrel Integration — A Practical Guide What each noise “type” actually is Construction public struct SquirrelNoise32Rng : IRandomFunction<uint, uint> public SquirrelNoise32Rng( uint seed, NoiseType type = NoiseType.MangledBitsBalancedMix, uint position = 0) // reset public void ResetSeed(uint seed, uint position = 0) Core settings public NoiseType Type { get; set; } public uint Seed { get; } // current seed public uint Position { get; } // current position (advances as you read values) Sampling API (per read advances Position) Scalars public float Value // [0,1] (float) public uint Uint32 public bool Bool public byte Byte public ushort Uint16 Ranged & chance helpers public float Range(float minInclusive, float maxInclusive) public int Range(int minInclusive, int maxExclusive) public bool Chance(float probabilityOfTrue) Vectors & directions public float2 Float2( float minX = float.MinValue, float maxX = float.MaxValue, float minY = float.MinValue, float maxY = float.MaxValue) public float3 Float3( float minX = float.MinValue, float maxX = float.MaxValue, float minY = float.MinValue, float maxY = float.MaxValue, float minZ = float.MinValue, float maxZ = float.MaxValue) public float4 Float4( float minX = float.MinValue, float maxX = float.MaxValue, float minY = float.MinValue, float maxY = float.MaxValue, float minZ = float.MinValue, float maxZ = float.MaxValue, float minW = float.MinValue, float maxW = float.MaxValue) public float2 Direction2D public float3 Direction3D public float2 InsideUnitCircle public float3 InsideUnitSphere public float3 OnUnitSphere Rotations public quaternion Rotation public quaternion RotationUniform Perlin helpers (seeded by this RNG) public float Perlin(float x, float y) public float Perlin(float x, float y, float z) All members above are pulled directly from SquirrelNoise32Rng.cs so signatures and defaults match the source. Examples using CoreFramework.Random; using Unity.Mathematics; var rng = new SquirrelNoise32Rng(seed: 1337U); // Scalars uint r = rng.Uint32; float u = rng.Value; bool hit = rng.Chance(0.1f); // Ranges int i = rng.Range(-10, 10); float f = rng.Range(-1f, 1f); // Vectors & rotations float3 dir = rng.Direction3D; float3 p = rng.InsideUnitSphere; quaternion q = rng.Rotation; // Perlin using the RNG’s seed/type float n2 = rng.Perlin(12.5f, 7.25f); float n3 = rng.Perlin(1f, 2f, 3f); Notes Deterministic for the same (Seed, Type) and read order; each getter advances Position internally. Designed for Burst: methods are small, inline-friendly, and allocation-free. Use ResetSeed(...) to reuse an RNG with a different seed and/or starting position. manual/code/Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise.title: SquirrelNoise64Bit | Unity 6 Core Framework
manual/code/Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise.summary: SquirrelNoise64Bit Source: ./Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise64Bit.cs Overview SquirrelNoise64Bit is the 64-bit, hash-based noise core for CoreFramework. It exposes fast, seedable 1D–4D integer noise returning ulong, normalized float variants ([0,1] and [-1,1]), Perlin wrappers (2D/3D with optional analytic derivatives), and Cellular/Worley helpers using 64-bit mixing. Defaults use DefaultNoiseType (currently MangledBitsBalancedMix) — see the guides below for details and trade-offs. Further reading: Noise Types & Squirrel Integration — A Practical Guide What each noise “type” actually is 64-bit integer noise public static ulong Get1DNoise(ulong index, ulong seed, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static ulong Get2DNoise(ulong x, ulong y, ulong seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static ulong Get3DNoise(ulong x, ulong y, ulong z, ulong seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static ulong Get4DNoise(ulong x, ulong y, ulong z, ulong w, ulong seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Returns component-hashed ulong values; stable across platforms for the same inputs. Normalized (0–1) Variants public static float Get1DNoise01(ulong index, ulong seed, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Get2DNoise01(ulong x, ulong y, ulong seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Get3DNoise01(ulong x, ulong y, ulong z, ulong seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Get4DNoise01(ulong x, ulong y, ulong z, ulong w, ulong seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Same as the integer cores but mapped to [0,1] float. Normalized (−1…1) Variants public static float Get1DNoiseNeg1To1(ulong index, ulong seed, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Get2DNoiseNeg1To1(ulong x, ulong y, ulong seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Get3DNoiseNeg1To1(ulong x, ulong y, ulong z, ulong seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Get4DNoiseNeg1To1(ulong x, ulong y, ulong z, ulong w, ulong seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Same cores, remapped to [-1,1] float. 128-bit helper public static ulong2 GetUInt128(ulong index, ulong seed, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Build combined 128-bit noise from the 64-bit core for wide keys and RNG state. Perlin noise (float domain) Scalar Perlin with corner-hashing done via the selected NoiseType. public static float Perlin(float x, float y, ulong seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float Perlin(float x, float y, float z, ulong seed = 0, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Perlin + analytic derivatives public static float PerlinWithDeriv(float x, float y, ulong seed, out float2 deriv, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float PerlinWithDeriv(float x, float y, float z, ulong seed, out float3 deriv, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) // Cell/offset overloads: public static float PerlinWithDeriv(float2 offset, int2 cell, ulong seed, out float2 deriv, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float PerlinWithDeriv(float3 offset, int3 cell, ulong seed, out float3 deriv, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Derivatives are computed analytically (not finite-differenced). Value noise with gradient public static float ValueAndGrad(float x, float y, ulong seed, out float2 grad, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float ValueAndGrad(float2 p, ulong seed, out float2 grad, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static float ValueAndGrad(float3 p, ulong seed, out float3 grad, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Cellular / Worley public static HashBasedNoiseUtils.Cellular2DResult Cellular2D( float x, float y, int frequency, ulong seed, float jitter = 0.9f, HashBasedNoiseUtils.CellularDistance metric = HashBasedNoiseUtils.CellularDistance.Euclidean, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) public static HashBasedNoiseUtils.Cellular3DResult Cellular3D( float x, float y, float z, int frequency, ulong seed, float jitter = 0.9f, HashBasedNoiseUtils.CellularDistance metric = HashBasedNoiseUtils.CellularDistance.Euclidean, NoiseType type = DefaultNoiseType) Returns nearest/second-nearest distances (F1, F2), feature position, and owning cell. See Cellular remaps and normalization helpers in HashBasedNoiseUtils. Examples using CoreFramework.Random; // integer ulong h = SquirrelNoise64Bit.Get3DNoise(12, 7, 4, seed: 1337UL); // normalized float float n = SquirrelNoise64Bit.Get2DNoise01(128UL, 64UL, seed: 42UL); // Perlin + derivative float v = SquirrelNoise64Bit.PerlinWithDeriv(3.2f, -1.1f, seed: 9UL, out float2 d); // wide keys ulong2 k128 = SquirrelNoise64Bit.GetUInt128(5UL, 99UL); Notes All methods are [MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining] and [BurstCompile] ready. Works statelessly — you can query any index without sequential calls. Use NoiseType to switch between bit-mix strategies (MangledBits, ChaCha, etc.). manual/code/Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise.title: SquirrelNoise64Rng | Unity 6 Core Framework
manual/code/Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise.summary: SquirrelNoise64Rng Source: ./Runtime/Random/SquirrelNoise64Rng.cs Overview SquirrelNoise64Rng is a lightweight, stateless-style RNG façade built on the 64-bit Squirrel noise core. Given a Seed and Position, it produces reproducible random values (scalars, vectors, rotations) by advancing the Position and hashing it with the chosen NoiseType. It’s ideal for deterministic gameplay, spawning, and procedural generation where you want repeatable streams without maintaining a heavy PRNG state. Defaults use NoiseType.ChaChaQuarterRoundSimple. See the guides for trade-offs and picking a noise type. Further reading: Noise Types & Squirrel Integration — A Practical Guide What each noise “type” actually is Construction public struct SquirrelNoise64Rng : IRandomFunction<ulong, ulong> public SquirrelNoise64Rng( ulong seed, NoiseType type = NoiseType.ChaChaQuarterRoundSimple, ulong position = 0) // reset public void ResetSeed(ulong seed, ulong position = 0) Core settings public NoiseType Type { get; set; } public ulong Seed { get; } // current seed public ulong Position { get; } // current position (advances as you read values) Sampling API (per read advances Position) Scalars public float Value // [0,1] (float) public ulong Uint64 public uint Uint32 public ushort Uint16 public byte Byte public bool Bool Ranged & chance helpers public float Range(float minInclusive, float maxInclusive) public int Range(int minInclusive, int maxExclusive) public bool Chance(float probabilityOfTrue) Vectors & directions public float2 Float2( float minX = float.MinValue, float maxX = float.MaxValue, float minY = float.MinValue, float maxY = float.MaxValue) public float3 Float3( float minX = float.MinValue, float maxX = float.MaxValue, float minY = float.MinValue, float maxY = float.MaxValue, float minZ = float.MinValue, float maxZ = float.MaxValue) public float4 Float4( float minX = float.MinValue, float maxX = float.MaxValue, float minY = float.MinValue, float maxY = float.MaxValue, float minZ = float.MinValue, float maxZ = float.MaxValue, float minW = float.MinValue, float maxW = float.MaxValue) public float2 Direction2D // unit vector uniformly distributed on the circle public float3 Direction3D // unit vector uniformly distributed on the sphere public float2 InsideUnitCircle public float3 InsideUnitSphere public float3 OnUnitSphere // alias for Direction3D Rotations public quaternion Rotation // uniform random rotation (unit quaternion) public quaternion RotationUniform // same: uniform on SO(3) Wide integers public ulong2 Uint128 Perlin helpers (seeded by this RNG) public float Perlin(float x, float y) public float Perlin(float x, float y, float z) All members above are pulled directly from SquirrelNoise64Rng.cs so signatures and defaults match the source. Examples using CoreFramework.Random; using Unity.Mathematics; var rng = new SquirrelNoise64Rng(seed: 1234UL); // Scalars uint r32 = rng.Uint32; ulong r64 = rng.Uint64; float u01 = rng.Value; bool hit = rng.Chance(0.25f); // Ranges int i = rng.Range(-10, 10); float f = rng.Range(-1f, 1f); // Vectors & rotations float3 dir = rng.Direction3D; float3 p = rng.InsideUnitSphere; quaternion q = rng.Rotation; // Wide ints ulong2 k = rng.Uint128; // Perlin using the RNG’s seed/type float n2 = rng.Perlin(12.5f, 7.25f); float n3 = rng.Perlin(1f, 2f, 3f); Notes Deterministic for the same (Seed, Type) and read order; each getter advances Position internally. Designed for Burst: methods are small, inline-friendly, and allocation-free. Use ResetSeed(...) to reuse an RNG with a different seed and/or starting position. manual/code/Runtime/Random/UniqueWorlds..title: How many different unique worlds? How big before repetition? | Unity 6 Core Framework
manual/code/Runtime/Random/UniqueWorlds..summary: How many different unique worlds? How big before repetition? If a “world” is fully determined by the seed, then the number of distinct worlds equals the number of distinct seeds because the noise is stateless and deterministic. 32-bit pipeline (uint seed): 2³² = 4,294,967,296 unique worlds 64-bit pipeline (ulong seed): 2⁶⁴ = 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 unique worlds (With our mixers, two different seeds producing the same infinite field would require a pathological collision across every index—practically zero, so count them all.) When does the world repeat? Two limits matter: 1) Exact tiling from the integer index combiner For integer hashing we build indices like 2D: i = x + P1*y (mod 2^N) 3D: i = x + P1*y + P2*z (mod 2^N) 4D: i = x + P1*y + P2*z + P3*w (mod 2^N) This gives true translational periods: small integer vectors (Δx,Δy,Δz,Δw) where the combination sums to 0 (mod 2^N). Using our constants: 32-bit (N=32, P1=198,491,317, P2=6,542,989, P3=357,239) 2D: period (P1, −1) → 198,491,317 cells 3D: period (P2, 0, −1) → 6,542,989 cells (shortest) 4D: period (P3, 0, 0, −1) → 357,239 cells (shortest) 64-bit (N=64, P1UL≈1.5486e19, P2UL≈1.4029e19, P3UL≈1.6096e18) 2D: (P1UL, −1) → ≈1.5486e19 cells 3D: (P2UL, 0, −1) → ≈1.4029e19 cells 4D: (P3UL, 0, 0, −1) → ≈1.6096e18 cells If you sample at frequency f (i.e., p_cell = p_world * f), the shortest repeat distance in world units along those vectors is: repeat_distance_world ≈ (period_in_cells) / f Examples (32-bit): 3D, f=1.0 → ~6.54 million units 3D, f=0.01 → ~654 million units 2D, f=0.01 → ~19.85 billion units 64-bit periods are astronomically large—you won’t hit them. 2) Floating-point precision (“detail horizon”) Unity/world space coords are float. A float has ~24 bits of mantissa, so beyond about 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 in the sampled coordinate space, adding ±1 no longer changes the value after the floor/fraction split used by Perlin/Simplex. In world units: detail_horizon_world ≈ 16,777,216 / f So at f=1.0, you keep 1-unit detail out to ~16.8M units. At f=0.01, it’s ~1.68B units. Which limit bites first? 32-bit hashing: the shortest tiling vector (e.g., 3D (P2,0,−1)) can be smaller than the float horizon at f=1. You could see repeats along that skew direction if you traverse that vector exactly. Along cardinal axes, periods are 2^32 cells—effectively unreachable. 64-bit hashing: the float horizon dominates by many orders of magnitude. You’ll hit precision limits long before any hash tiling. Recommended max int3 worldSize Assume your loops visit all integer cells from -worldSize to +worldSize inclusive (so 2*W+1 samples per axis) and step size = 1 cell. ⚠️ Axis reminder (important) Your current call is Perlin( y, x, z, seed ). The 3D index is idx = X + P1*Y + P2*Z. That means world Y → hash X, which is the axis that repeats fastest. Clamp the small bound on world Y with this call order. If you switch to Perlin(x,y,z), move the small bound to world X instead. Using the 32-bit pipeline (e.g., SquirrelNoise32Bit) If you sample Perlin/Simplex anywhere (floats involved): Anisotropic safe (with Perlin(y,x,z)): worldSize = int3(8_388_607, 3_271_494, 8_388_607) Cube option: worldSize = int3(3_271_494) (Numbers come from: shortest 3D period (P2,0,−1) ⇒ keep 2*W_small+1 < P2 → W_small ≤ floor((P2−1)/2) = 3,271,494; and float horizon W ≤ (2^24−1)/2 = 8,388,607 per float axis.) If you only use integer hash/value noise (no floats): Anisotropic max (with Perlin(y,x,z)): worldSize = int3(int.MaxValue, 3_271_494, int.MaxValue) (practically choose smaller for memory/perf) Cube option: int3(3_271_494) Using the 64-bit pipeline (e.g., SquirrelNoise64Bit) If you sample Perlin/Simplex: worldSize = int3(8_388_607) (float horizon dominates) If you only use integer hashing/value noise: Effectively unbounded within int; choose by memory/perf. Frequency scaling If you pre-scale positions by frequency f before Perlin/Simplex: Float-limited axes (X/Z here): W ≤ floor(8_388_607 / f) Small 32-bit axis (Y here): W ≤ floor(3_271_494 / f) You can exceed these in practice with origin rebasing (keep the active window near 0 in world→noise space), while keeping 64-bit hashing for stability. Loop skeleton (inclusive bounds + correct small axis on Y) const int FloatHorizon = 8_388_607; // (2^24 - 1)/2 const int Small32 = 3_271_494; // floor((P2 - 1)/2), P2 = 6,542,989 // Current call order Perlin(y,x,z): small bound goes on Y. var worldSize32 = new int3(FloatHorizon, Small32, FloatHorizon); var worldSize64 = new int3(FloatHorizon); var W = use32Bit ? worldSize32 : worldSize64; // Inclusive loops → 2*W+1 samples per axis. for (int z = -W.z; z <= W.z; z++) for (int x = -W.x; x <= W.x; x++) for (int y = -W.y; y <= W.y; y++) { float n = use32Bit ? SquirrelNoise32Bit.Perlin( y, x, z, seed ) // note (y,x,z) : SquirrelNoise64Bit.Perlin( y, x, z, seed ); } 64-bit negative-cast tip When implementing SquirrelNoise64Bit.Perlin, compute lattice coordinates as signed first, then cast to ulong for hashing: long xi = (long)math.floor(x), yi = (long)math.floor(y), zi = (long)math.floor(z); float xf = x - xi, yf = y - yi, zf = z - zi; var h000 = SquirrelNoise64Bit.Get3DNoise( unchecked((ulong)xi), unchecked((ulong)yi), unchecked((ulong)zi), seed); Casting a negative directly to ulong before subtracting the integer part will break the fractional offsets. How does this compare to UnityEngine.Mathf.PerlinNoise(x, z)? Short answer: Mathf.PerlinNoise is a handy 2D, seedless, engine-side Perlin with a small, fixed period; Squirrel-based noise is seeded, Burst-friendly, supports 3D, huge periods, and extras like derivatives and cellular. Unity’s Mathf.PerlinNoise 2D only, signature PerlinNoise(float x, float y) → returns [0,1]. No seed (to vary results you offset/scale inputs). Deterministic for same inputs. True period ≈ 256 cells per axis, because classic Perlin uses a 256-entry permutation table. With sampling frequency f, the world-space repeat is ≈ 256 / f. Float precision horizon still exists (~16,777,216 / f), but the 256/f period is the much tighter limit. Not Burst/job friendly (lives in UnityEngine; can’t call it from Burst jobs). No derivatives; gradients require extra samples. Squirrel Noise pipeline 2D & 3D Perlin (and Simplex, Cellular), all stateless and seeded. 32-bit seeds: 2^32 worlds. 64-bit seeds: 2^64 worlds. Huge periods from integer hashing: in 3D (32-bit) the shortest repeat vector is ~6,542,989 cells (directional), vs 256 for Mathf. In 64-bit, repeats are effectively unreachable; float precision dominates. Burst-friendly, job-safe; analytic derivatives available. Plus Worley/Cellular, ridge/billow stacks, domain warps, etc. Quick repeat math vs Unity Let f be the frequency multiplied into world coords before sampling. Unity 2D Perlin: Repeat distance: ~256 / f (hard limit) Precision horizon: ~16,777,216 / f (larger; usually irrelevant) If you loop -W .. +W inclusive, keep 2W+1 < 256/f ⇒ W ≤ floor((256/f - 1)/2). Squirrel 3D Perlin (32-bit): Shortest repeat: ~6,542,989 / f (skew direction) Float horizon: ~16,777,216 / f per axis Use the smaller of those for a conservative bound. Squirrel 3D Perlin (64-bit): Repeat: effectively unreachable; float horizon wins. If you “fake 3D” with Mathf.PerlinNoise You can blend slices, but expect axis bias and the same 256/f repeat: // crude “3D” blend of three 2D slices; still repeats every 256/f float Perlin3D_Fake(float x, float y, float z, float f) { float a = Mathf.PerlinNoise(x*f, z*f); float b = Mathf.PerlinNoise(x*f + 37.2f, y*f + 11.5f); float c = Mathf.PerlinNoise(y*f + 19.7f, z*f + 53.8f); return (a + b + c) / 3f * 2f - 1f; // map to ~[-1,1] } Bottom line: for big worlds, 3D, seeds, jobs/Burst, and advanced compositions (derivatives, warps, cellular), the Squirrel Noise pipeline is clearly the better foundation. TL;DR Unique worlds: 32-bit 2^32, 64-bit 2^64. Practical non-repeat span: min( tiling distance, float horizon ) / f. With Perlin(y,x,z), clamp Y to 3,271,494 (32-bit) and keep X/Z to 8,388,607. For a cube: int3(3,271,494) (32-bit) or int3(8,388,607) (64-bit). Unity’s Mathf.PerlinNoise repeats every ~256/f units; great for small 2D uses, not for large 3D worlds.

manual/code/Runtime/Settings/CoreFramewo.title: CoreFrameworkSettings | Unity 6 Core Framework
manual/code/Runtime/Settings/CoreFramewo.summary: CoreFrameworkSettings Source: ./Runtime/Settings/CoreFrameworkSettings.cs Overview A runtime static container that other systems read to determine startup scenes and debug display preferences. Values are populated in the Editor by CoreFrameworkSettingInitialization, which mirrors: Project-wide scene choices from CoreFrameworkProjectSettings Per-developer debug prefs from CoreFrameworkPreferences These values are then consumed at runtime (e.g., by Bootstrapper). Fields (defaults shown) public static class CoreFrameworkSettings { /// Name of the game start scene. "None" disables loading. public static string StartScene = "None"; /// Name of the boot scene. "None" disables loading. public static string BootScene = "None"; /// Show debug messages controlled by CoreFramework utilities. public static bool ShowDebug; /// Rich-text font sizes for info/warn/error logs. public static int InfoSize = 14; public static int WarningSize = 15; public static int ErrorSize = 16; } In the Editor, these are set on load from the Preferences/Project Settings. In a built player, set them via your own bootstrap/config if needed. Typical usage Scene boot flow (used by Bootstrapper) // Boot scene load (simplified) if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(CoreFrameworkSettings.BootScene) && !string.Equals(CoreFrameworkSettings.BootScene, "None", StringComparison.Ordinal)) { SceneManager.LoadScene(CoreFrameworkSettings.BootScene); } // Start scene load (built player path) if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(CoreFrameworkSettings.StartScene) && !string.Equals(CoreFrameworkSettings.StartScene, "None", StringComparison.Ordinal)) { SceneManager.LoadSceneAsync(CoreFrameworkSettings.StartScene, LoadSceneMode.Additive); } Consistent debug formatting (pair with your own base class) using UnityEngine; public abstract class CoreFrameworkDebugBehaviour : MonoBehaviour { protected void LogInfo(string message, Object ctx = null) { if (CoreFrameworkSettings.ShowDebug) Debug.Log($"<size={CoreFrameworkSettings.InfoSize}><color=blue>Info:</color> {message}</size>", ctx); } protected void LogWarning(string message, Object ctx = null) { if (CoreFrameworkSettings.ShowDebug) Debug.LogWarning($"<size={CoreFrameworkSettings.WarningSize}><color=orange>Warning:</color> {message}</size>", ctx); } protected void LogError(string message, Object ctx = null) { Debug.LogError($"<size={CoreFrameworkSettings.ErrorSize}><color=red>Error:</color> {message}</size>", ctx); } } Notes Editor population: Happens via [InitializeOnLoad] in CoreFrameworkSettingInitialization. Build settings: Scene names must be listed in File → Build Settings… to load by name. Team vs. personal: StartScene/BootScene come from Project Settings (team-shared). ShowDebug/sizes come from Preferences (per-developer). Related Pages Bootstrapper CoreFrameworkSettingInitialization CoreFrameworkProjectSettings CoreFrameworkPreferences Related API xref:CoreFramework.Settings.CoreFrameworkSettings

manual/code/Runtime/Settings/VersionCont.title: VersionControl | Unity 6 Core Framework
manual/code/Runtime/Settings/VersionCont.summary: VersionControl Source: ./Runtime/Settings/VersionControl.cs (runtime) Overview A lightweight runtime container that tracks the project’s file/version information: CurrentFileVersion — the version your content/save format is currently at. MinFileVersion — the earliest version still considered compatible. These values are set from editor data at load time: VersionInitialization copies values from VersionProjectSettings into VersionControl. Changing VersionProjectSettings.CurrentFileVersion or .MinFileVersion also writes into VersionControl (via the property setters shown on that page). Unity’s PlayerSettings.bundleVersion is kept in sync by VersionInitialization and by the VersionProjectSettings.CurrentFileVersion setter. Fields // System.Version values (Major.Minor.Build.Revision) public static Version CurrentFileVersion; // latest supported version public static Version MinFileVersion; // minimum backward-compatible version These are System.Version values, so you can compare them directly with <, >, ==, etc. Typical usage Gate loading by version Use the min/current values to validate save data, content packs, or networked payloads. using System; bool IsSaveSupported(Version saveVersion) { // Must be >= minimum AND <= current return saveVersion >= VersionControl.MinFileVersion && saveVersion <= VersionControl.CurrentFileVersion; } Example: save header check [Serializable] public struct SaveHeader { public string productName; public string guid; public string version; // serialized as string "2.0.0.0" } bool TryValidate(SaveHeader header, out string reason) { if (!Version.TryParse(header.version, out var v)) { reason = "Invalid version format."; return false; } if (v < VersionControl.MinFileVersion) { reason = $"Save too old. Min supported: {VersionControl.MinFileVersion}"; return false; } if (v > VersionControl.CurrentFileVersion) { reason = $"Save from newer build. Current: {VersionControl.CurrentFileVersion}"; return false; } reason = null; return true; } Bumping versions (editor-driven) You normally bump versions via editor UI and build menus: Project Settings → Core Framework → Version Settings (VersionProjectSettingsProvider) edits the numbers. Core Framework → Build → (0..3) (BuildProcessing) increments parts and applies to VersionProjectSettings.CurrentFileVersion. Those flows then update VersionControl automatically. Notes VersionControl is read at runtime; values are written from editor-side systems. In Player builds, ensure your save/load code writes a version string/number that can be parsed to System.Version. If you need custom compatibility rules (e.g., allow specific hotfix revisions), implement those checks on top of these two values. Related Pages VersionInitialization VersionProjectSettings BuildProcessing Related API xref:CoreFramework.Settings.VersionControl xref:CoreFramework.Settings.VersionProjectSettings xref:CoreFramework.Settings.VersionProjectSettingsProvider
